## Overview

Grapevine leafroll disease is caused by viruses that mealybugs carry from vine
to vine along the trellis. An infected vine yields less and worse fruit for
the rest of its life. Infection stays invisible for a year or more, so
roguing symptomatic vines may come too late. @Atallah2015 built a vine-level
cellular automaton of a vineyard with an economic layer. They compared
eighteen strategies of roguing, replanting and virus-testing by their
expected net present value (ENPV) over 50 years. Their finding is that
testing the neighbours of each symptomatic vine pays, by about 18%, while
roguing alone does not.

The journal article is behind a paywall, so this model follows Chapter 2 of
the first author's dissertation [@Atallah2014], which reports the same design
and results. It is an **adaptation**. The sources leave unstated when a
symptomatic vine is found and what state the first infections start in, and
those choices move the results.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Statistics
```

## The model

A 5.2-acre vineyard has 44 trellis rows of 130 vines. Each vine is healthy,
exposed but undetectable, exposed and detectable, infective-moderate or
infective-high, and has an age in months. Each month:

- a healthy vine is infected at rate 4.2 per infective neighbour along its
  trellis row and 0.014 per infective neighbour in the next rows;
- an infected vine stays undetectable for 4 to 18 months (triangular, mode 12);
- an exposed-detectable vine becomes infective-moderate at a mean of 24, 48
  or 72 months for young, mature or old vines;
- infective-moderate becomes infective-high at a mean of 36 months.

A vine earns from 36 months of age: $0.43 a month if healthy, less if
infected (30%, 50% or 75% less yield and 10% less in price). Roguing and
replanting costs $7.25 and a virus test $2.61, discounted at 0.9959 a month.

```{julia}
model = build(:grapevine_leafroll)
```

## The economics without disease

Without disease the vineyard's value is fixed. It is the check on the age and
time conventions:

```{julia}
nodisease = grapevine_npv(solve(problem(:grapevine_leafroll; infected=0.0)))
round(nodisease / 1000; digits=1)
```

That is the source's $463k.

## Spread without control

Two per cent of the vines start infected. Transmission along a trellis row is
almost certain within a month of a neighbour becoming infective, and across
rows it is rare. But a newly infected vine takes about three years, on
average, to become infective itself. That slows the spread along a row to a
few vines a decade, and over the same decades the rare jumps across rows add
up, so the patches grow in both directions:

```{julia}
sol = solve(problem(:grapevine_leafroll; seed=2); saveat=120)
vinemap(u, title) = heatmap(u.state; c=[:forestgreen, :khaki, :orange, :firebrick, :black],
                            clims=(0, 4), colorbar=false, framestyle=:none, title,
                            aspect_ratio=0.5)
plot([vinemap(u, "month $t") for (t, u) in zip(sol.t, sol.u)]...; layout=(1, 6),
     size=(1000, 330))
```

Each column is a trellis row. Healthy vines are green, exposed vines yellow
(undetectable) or orange (detectable), and infective vines red (moderate) or
black (high).

The vineyard's half-life is the time until half the vines are infected. The
source reports 188 months without control:

```{julia}
halflives = [grapevine_half_life(solve(problem(:grapevine_leafroll; seed=s))) for s in 1:20]
(mean=mean(halflives), sd=round(std(halflives); digits=1))
```

The disease is slower here, by about four years.

## Strategies

The source's Table 2.5 gives the ENPV of each strategy over 1000 runs. Twenty
runs each here, for the main ones:

- `:none`: no control.
- `:I`, `:Ih`: rogue all infective, or only infective-high, vines.
- `:ImY`: rogue infective-moderate young vines.
- `:ImNS`, `:ImNSEW`: rogue each infective-moderate vine and test its two
  neighbours along the row (or all four neighbours), roguing those found
  exposed-detectable.
- `:ImNS2EW`: also test the second neighbours along the row.

```{julia}
strategies = (:none, :I, :Ih, :ImY, :ImNS, :ImNSEW, :ImNS2EW)
source = Dict(:none => 316, :I => -147, :Ih => 284, :ImY => 314, :ImNS => 374,
              :ImNSEW => 374, :ImNS2EW => 309)
enpv(strategy; runs=20, kw...) = [grapevine_npv(solve(problem(:grapevine_leafroll; strategy,
                                                              seed=s, kw...)))
                                  for s in 1:runs] ./ 1000
results = Dict(st => enpv(st) for st in strategies)
[(strategy=st, model=round(mean(results[st])), sd=round(std(results[st]); digits=1),
  source=source[st]) for st in strategies]
```

Testing the neighbours along the row comes out as in the source: about $382k
against $374k, a gain over no control. Roguing infective-high vines alone
loses value, as in the source. Several results differ:

- With the slower epidemic, no control is worth more than in the source.
- Testing the second neighbours along the row is worth as much as testing
  the first, where the source finds it costs more than it saves.
- Roguing young symptomatic vines gains a little, where the source finds it
  loses a little.
- Roguing every infective vine, which the source finds ruinous at −$147k, is
  as good here as the spatial strategies.

## Choices the source leaves open

The source does not say when a symptomatic vine is found and rogued. By
default it is rogued after it has been infective for one month, so it infects
its row neighbours first (`delay = 1`). With `delay = 0` it is rogued as soon
as it shows symptoms, and the spatial strategies look much better than they
do in the source:

```{julia}
[(strategy=st, delay_0=round(mean(enpv(st; runs=10, delay=0))),
  delay_1=round(mean(results[st]))) for st in (:none, :I, :ImNS)]
```

The first infections are "exposed" in the source, which does not say whether
they can be detected. Starting them infective (`initial = :Im`) brings the
half-life and the no-control value close to the source's (188 months and
$316k). But testing neighbours then gains much less than in the source:

```{julia}
hl_im = [grapevine_half_life(solve(problem(:grapevine_leafroll; initial=:Im, seed=s)))
         for s in 1:20]
(half_life=mean(hl_im),
 none=round(mean(enpv(:none; runs=10, initial=:Im))),
 ImNS=round(mean(enpv(:ImNS; runs=10, initial=:Im))))
```

No reading tried reproduces every row of the source's table. Most of all,
none makes roguing every infective vine as costly as it is in the source.
